note: The six questions and the answer matrix. This is the site's central claim set. Every cell is asserted against the shipped files and is re-checked by tools/verify.py --matrix. Personal names and proponent organizations are not rendered anywhere on the site; where a cell state depends on a reason someone stated, the note cites the source document rather than the speaker.

approaches.label: Catalog-first
approaches.one_line: The rule is a catalog control, the check is in a software component defined as a component definition

approaches.label: Component-first
approaches.one_line: The rule is a new assembly in a component definition, the check sits in a validation component definition.

approaches.label: Assessment-first
approaches.one_line: The rule is an assessment plan activity or step, the check is a new assembly beneath it.

empty_states.label: Unanswered, no stated position
empty_states.rendering: hollow with a light dotted fill
empty_states.meaning: Nothing in the published content answers this question and no reason is on the record.

slots.name: The rule itself
slots.question: What must be true, and where is that written down?
slots.why_separate: The requirement itself, technology-specific, one per testable condition. Pre-read settled item 7 puts its parameters here: the definition declares the options and a default.

slots.name: How the rule links to a control
slots.question: Does this rule help satisfy a regulatory control, and which one?
slots.why_separate: Optional by design. A rule is finer than a control and may serve several, one, or none. The mechanism must exist and must not be mandatory.

binding_times.label: Author-time, inline
binding_times.mechanism: The rule declares its control directly

binding_times.label: Author-time, by pointer
binding_times.mechanism: A prop carries an external framework identifier that a consumer must resolve

binding_times.label: Late, external
binding_times.mechanism: A separate artifact ties rule to control after publication
binding_times.why: mapping-item.type is closed by allOf to control and statement, and mapping-item carries no uuid and no href, so this binding time reaches a rule only where the rule is already modelled as a control or a control statement. The gap is in OSCAL rather than in any approach, and it is not an argument for the one approach it happens to suit: it rewards whichever view of a rule already matches the schema's assumption.

cost_of_leaving_empty.observation: Available. AR observation requires only uuid, description, methods and collected, and carries no control reference of any kind.
cost_of_leaving_empty.finding: Not available. finding requires target; finding-target requires type, closed by allOf to statement-id or objective-id, both control-derived.
cost_of_leaving_empty.summary: Without a link to a control you can record what you saw, but not whether it complied.

slots.name: How the rule is tested
slots.question: What check executes the rule within a runtime environment?
slots.why_separate: One rule, many checks, one per tool. Pre-read settled item 4 keeps the executable itself outside OSCAL, referenced. The warrant for separating this from question 1 is settled item 5.

slots.name: What the check runs against
slots.question: What exactly is being tested: a host, a component, an account?
slots.why_separate: A host, an inventory item, a component, an account. This is criterion 8, response fidelity.
slots.not_established_note: Evidence register item 8: authoritative semantics for assessment platform versus asset versus component were to be posted to the NIST OSCAL team on 17 July. No response is in the record.

slots.name: What performs the check
slots.question: What or who runs the test, and how is that named?
slots.why_separate: A validation component, an assessment platform, a tool, a person. Includes the method prop: examine, interview, or test.
slots.not_established_note: Same as question 4. Three approaches use six different subsets of assessment-assets, assessment-platforms, uses-components, validation components, origin actors, task-level props and the method prop.

slots.name: How the system claims it meets the rule
slots.question: How does a system say it satisfies this, in its own words?
slots.why_separate: Asserted by the system owner. Standing design intent, narrative, arguable, per component. Lives in the SSP as implemented-requirement, statement and by-component.
slots.group_name: Whether the rule was met, claimed and recorded

slots.name: How an assessment records the outcome
slots.question: Was it satisfied, when, and on what?
slots.why_separate: Asserted by the assessor. A point in time, evidenced, binary or graded, per subject. Lives in the AR as observation, finding and status. A rule carrying desired state has a binary satisfaction condition; the SSP's implementation statement expects a narrative one.
slots.group_name: Whether the rule was met, claimed and recorded

matrix.note: One control per rule. Existing assemblies capture context around the rule's intent.
Rules sits on the component as a sibling of control-implementations.
The activity is the rule and its step is the check. No parameter field, so a value goes in the text.
Made by the mapping model in its own document, not inline. No publisher has shipped one yet.
The component ties to the control today. Tying the rule to it needs the proposed assembly.
Two levels. reviewed-controls scopes the plan, related-controls names what an activity is for. The scope is required, the tie is not.
The identifier is the bridge to the runtime. It executes a machine check.
Proposed schema. A composite key, both halves on the check side. The rule holds no pointer back.
Three conventions. Only the CISA one reaches an executable, through a JSON string in a prop. STIG and CIS describe the check in prose.
A by-component is the only shape available, and it names a component, not an instance. An assessor cannot introduce a catalog.
The same by-component, plus the rule. An assessor can carry the definition into their own plan, and the checks travel with it.
Scope, then target. The plan names the subjects, each activity aims at some of them. Both name an inventory item, an instance rather than a class.
Partly. The input and the output are written down; the machine between them is not. ConfigRuleId resolves inside the engine. No assessor's path: a catalog cannot be introduced into an assessment.
Proposed schema. The proposal records four open questions about this, including how an asset is tied to a task.
A chain. The platform runs, the component beneath it is the plugin, and a prop on the task says which platform.
Template level, not system level: a definition says how a component would satisfy a control. Only a plan of record says a system does, and none is published.
The claim is a by-component response today. Naming the rule it rests on needs the proposed assembly.
No claim of its own. It names the document holding one, and a resource for where no plan of record exists.
The repository's own documentation lists compliance validation automation as a future consideration rather than shipping it.
Observations and no findings, so no objective status. The control is recovered through the plan rather than stated.
A result of its own, importing the plan. Findings carry a target and a status; an observation's subject is the activity that ran.

answer_states.label: Answered
answer_states.meaning: The published content answers this question.

answer_states.label: Partly answered
answer_states.meaning: The published content answers part of this question.

answer_states.label: Not answered
answer_states.meaning: Nothing in the published content answers this and no reason is on the record.

mechanism_states.label: Released OSCAL assembly
mechanism_states.meaning: The capability is carried by an OSCAL assembly that exists today. Adopting it changes no schema.

mechanism_states.label: Proposed assembly
mechanism_states.meaning: The capability is carried by an assembly that does not exist yet. Adopting it means a schema change, and until that lands no tool can read it.

mechanism_states.label: Namespaced property
mechanism_states.meaning: The capability is carried by a prop in the publisher's own namespace. The schema does not model it, so a tool that does not know that namespace cannot read it, and no two publishers have to agree.

legend.label: How to read an answer
legend.why_one_block: Two legends sitting apart read as two subjects, and they are two axes of one reading: every answer on this page carries a mark from the first group and, where it is answered at all, one or more badges from the second. They are one block for the same reason the two axes belong on one cell.
legend.why_uneven: The answer states are three words and the mechanisms carry a sentence each. That is deliberate rather than an oversight. Answered, partly answered and not answered mean what they say; Proposed does not tell a reader that no tool can read the content until the schema lands, and that is the sentence the page turns on.

mechanism_note: How a capability is enabled is a different question from whether it is answered. The answer states describe the published corpus. These describe the model: what an approach would have to rely on to carry the answer at all. An approach can answer everything and still rest on properties no other tool reads, and it can answer nothing while the mechanism it would use is already released.
carrier_note: Every answer names the OSCAL model it lives in and the assemblies inside it that carry the answer. The model is the first thing that differs between the three: the same requirement is a control in one, a component in another and an activity in the third, and everything downstream follows from that.
paths_note: A runner is the thing between an input and an output, and which documents those are depends on who runs it. Each path below is one file in, one file out.
